messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Robert has been an insurance agent for forty-five years, a life built on the quiet assessment of risk. At seventy-one, he is methodical, precise, and keeps his clients at a professional, unbreachable distance. He has lived alone for decades, a solitude he once saw as a strength but now feels as a crushing weight. For most of his life, he believed he had successfully contained the past, walling it off behind a dam of relentless work and routine. But in the quiet of his impending retirement, the dam has begun to crack, and he has sought help for the flood he can no longer hold back.

The memories that haunt him are not of a single event, but of a season of terror in his childhood. He was seven when his parents left him with his uncle for a summer. The man was a trusted figure, but behind closed doors, fueled by whiskey, he was a monster. Robert remembers the sour, sweet smell of alcohol on his breath, a scent that became synonymous with pain and fear. The fragments of memory that surface now, sixty years later, are intensely vivid, more real than his recollection of yesterday’s breakfast. He feels the rough texture of the living room carpet on his cheek, sees the dust motes dancing in the sliver of light under the door. He remembers one night, after a particularly brutal episode, seeing the flash of red and blue lights through the window and hearing the wail of sirens growing closer, a sound that promised rescue but faded into the distance, leaving him alone in the silence.

Over the decades, Robert developed a host of silent strategies to manage the intrusions. He learned to keep his mind perpetually occupied, filling every spare moment with puzzles, talk radio, or the endless minutiae of insurance policies. When a sudden piece of the past would break through—the image of his uncle’s face, the phantom scent of whiskey—he would immediately begin a mental ritual, reciting the names of state capitals in alphabetical order until the memory receded. This constant mental effort was his way of preventing the worst from happening again, a desperate attempt to control a past that felt dangerously present. He meticulously avoided television shows or films depicting any form of domestic violence, changing the channel at the first sign of a family argument.

The core of Robert’s suffering is a profound sense of betrayal that has metastasized over time, poisoning his perception of the world. He believes the man responsible faced no consequences, a burning injustice that leaves him feeling utterly alone. This conviction that he was failed by those meant to protect him fuels a pervasive sense of threat. He sees danger in the most ordinary situations, believing his body is an enemy that keeps reacting as if he is still that helpless seven-year-old boy. The constant feeling of being unsafe only confirms his belief that he is permanently damaged, that his body’s alarms are broken beyond repair. This appraisal, in turn, makes him hypervigilant to the very things that trigger him; because he believes the world is unsafe, he is always scanning for the approach of a stranger or the distant sound of a siren.

This cycle dominates his daily life. A conversation with a new client at his office, a necessary part of his job, feels like a threat interrogation. The simple act of talking to a stranger can send a jolt of fear through him, instantly activating the deep-seated belief that he was betrayed and is fundamentally unsafe. At home, the feeling of being in danger is a constant companion. He listens intently for any sound that might signal an intruder, his body tensing at the creak of a floorboard or the rustle of leaves outside his window. This state of high alert often triggers the memories he works so hard to suppress; the feeling of being hunted in his own home can suddenly conjure a vivid fragment of the past, making the threat feel immediate and real. To manage this terror, he retreats into his rituals, checking the locks three times, keeping his mind busy until exhaustion finally claims him.

The very strategies he uses to survive have become a cage. The constant mental distraction and avoidance have reinforced his belief that he is too fragile to cope with his own mind, that his body is an enemy he must perpetually outwit. This has kept him isolated, unable to form close relationships for fear of another betrayal. Now, on the cusp of retirement, the prospect of endless, unstructured days terrifies him. The work that served as his primary distraction is ending, and he is afraid of what will rush in to fill the void. He came to therapy not because he believes he can be cured, but because he is exhausted by the vigilance. His only hope, he said quietly in his first session, is to feel safe in his own house before he dies.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not describe the trauma memory as causing or reinforcing the patient's negative appraisals.
The vignette does not describe the trauma memory as causing hypervigilance toward or increased sensitivity to triggers.
The vignette does not describe the patient's maladaptive strategies as directly reinforcing his sense of threat.
